title: Candle Inclusion
summary: When one candle's range swallows its neighbor, merge them into one before anything else
body:
**The diagram**

The second candle in the box has a lower high and a higher low than the first, so it sits entirely inside it. That's an inclusion. On the right is the merged result.

**Textbook definition**

• When one candle's high and low fully contain the next one's, the two are in an inclusion relationship. You can't tell which is the real high or low, so they're merged into one.
• The merge direction follows the move **before** them: in a rise, take the higher high and the higher low; in a decline, take the lower high and the lower low.
• Merging repeats until no neighbors contain each other. Fractals, strokes and segments are all built on the merged candles.

**How this app does it**

• Same rule, handled automatically by the open-source Chan engine we use.
• All prices are **dividend/split-adjusted**, so gaps caused by payouts or splits aren't mistaken for real structure.
• The chart still draws the original candles while structure lines sit on the merged ones, so an endpoint occasionally won't line up with a wick. That's expected. The first few candles before the first stroke completes aren't used.

title: Fractal
summary: Three candles where the middle one is highest (top) or lowest (bottom) — the endpoints of a stroke
body:
**The diagram**

The three candles on the left form a top fractal: the middle one has both the highest high and the highest low. The three on the right form a bottom fractal, the mirror image.

**Textbook definition**

• Top fractal: of three consecutive (merged) candles, the middle one has the highest high and also the highest low.
• Bottom fractal: the middle one has the lowest low and also the lowest high.
• Both conditions must hold. A fractal is only a possible turning point, not a trade signal; a new high (or low) afterwards cancels it.

**How this app does it**

• Same rule, computed by the open-source engine.
• The chart only marks fractals that **became stroke endpoints** (top red, bottom green). Candidates that never produced a stroke can be overturned at any time; showing them all just adds clutter.
• A fractal whose right-hand candle has no newer candle after it is marked unconfirmed.

title: Stroke
summary: A line from one fractal to the next opposite fractal — the first Chan structure with a direction
body:
**The diagram**

From the bottom fractal (green dot) to the top fractal (red dot) is one up-stroke. The dashed line at the far right is the last stroke: it's still moving and its end can keep extending.

**Textbook definition**

• A stroke joins a top and a bottom: bottom to top is an up-stroke, top to bottom a down-stroke.
• The two fractals can't share candles, and there must be at least one independent candle between them, so small wiggles don't count.
• An up-stroke must end higher than it starts, and vice versa. If price keeps making new highs (or lows), the stroke extends.

**How this app does it**

• Computed by the open-source engine with a slightly looser rule: the two fractals just can't share candles, so a stroke spans at least **6** merged candles. The two fractals' price ranges also can't contain each other.
• A stroke ends at the furthest fractal: the highest top for an up-stroke, the lowest bottom for a down-stroke.
• **The last stroke is always unconfirmed** and drawn dashed.

title: Segment
summary: A larger move made of at least three strokes that filters out the back-and-forth noise
body:
**The diagram**

Five blue strokes go up and down, but the whole thing keeps climbing. Together they form one orange up-segment.

**Textbook definition**

• A segment has at least three strokes, and the first three must overlap in price. Its direction is set by the first stroke.
• A segment ends when the opposite side forms a "feature-sequence fractal". Put simply, the counter-move gets strong enough to make a turn of its own.
• When there's a price gap, you need to wait for a few more strokes to confirm the end.

**How this app does it**

• Segments are built in-house and handle both feature-sequence cases; with a gap, the app looks a few strokes further before deciding, so segments aren't cut short.
• Segments connect end to end, and each one ends at its own extreme (highest point for an up-segment, lowest for a down-segment). If price takes back the segment's starting point, the segment is over.
• The last segment is marked unconfirmed until later moves confirm it.
• Reading tip: check the segment direction first, then the stroke details.

title: Pivot
summary: The overlap of at least three strokes — where bulls and bears fight, and how you tell a range from a trend
body:
**The diagram**

The purple box is a pivot: three strokes swing back and forth inside this range. Then one stroke leaves upward, and the pullback doesn't fall back into the box, so the bulls have the upper hand.

**Textbook definition**

• A pivot is the **overlapping range** of at least three consecutive moves.
• Pivot top = the lowest of the first three highs; pivot bottom = the highest of the first three lows.
• While price keeps coming back into the range, the pivot extends. Once price leaves and doesn't return, it's over.
• One pivot means a **range**. Two pivots stepping higher (or lower) without overlapping means a **trend**.

**How this app does it**

• Pivots are built on strokes by the open-source engine: at least 3 strokes with a real overlap. The top and bottom are fixed by the first three strokes; extensions only update the highest and lowest points.
• The trend chip on the page reads the pivot layout: no pivot = structure not formed; one pivot, or pivots that overlap = consolidation; each pivot fully above the last = uptrend; the reverse = downtrend.
• The pivot-stage badge shows where things stand: pivot forming → oscillating → leaving the pivot → buy/sell point confirmed → divergence / turn.
• No higher-level pivot is computed on the same chart. To see the bigger picture, switch to weekly.

title: Divergence
summary: Price makes a new high (or low) but the push behind it is weaker — a hint not to chase
body:
**The diagram**

Two up-moves. The second one makes a new high, but it rises much less than the first. The pink line connects the two ends; 0.58 means the second move's price range is only 0.58× the first.

**Textbook definition**

• Compare two moves in the same direction: if the later one makes a new high (or low) with less force, that's divergence.
• The two moves must be the same level and direction, with a pivot or a counter-move between them.
• Divergence after two or more pivots is **trend divergence**; divergence around a single pivot is **range divergence**. The first is more reliable.
• Force is often measured by MACD area, or simply by move size and speed.
• **Divergence is not a reversal.** It only says the current direction is running out of steam; price may just go sideways and then continue.

**How this app does it**

• Uses the textbook measure: **MACD bar area**.
• The Strict rule only counts **trend divergence**: two pivots already formed, moving the same way without overlapping. The c leg (leaving the later pivot) is compared with the b leg (between the two pivots). A smaller c-leg area plus a new high (low) is divergence, and corresponds to a type-1 buy / sell. Range divergence does not count.
• The default Balanced rule also counts **range divergence** as a type-1 buy / sell (about twice as many signals), and Relaxed counts even more. Switch under Me → Preferences → Signal rules, where each rule is explained.
• No strength tiers: it either holds or it doesn't (the area ratio showed no stable link to what followed).
• On the chart, the b leg and the c leg are drawn as two pink lines, with "Trend div + area ratio" labeled on the c leg.

title: MACD (a common divergence tool)
summary: Many people use it to gauge divergence, but it isn't native to Chan, and this app doesn't use it for decisions
body:
**The diagram**

Price tops out and falls. Below it, the MACD red bars first grow, then shrink, then turn green.

**What it is**

• **DIF** (blue): the gap between a fast and a slow moving average, showing how far short-term price has moved from the medium term.
• **DEA** (orange): a moving average of DIF, smoother and slower.
• **Bars**: DIF minus DEA. Longer red bars = the move is accelerating; shorter = slowing (not the same as falling); red turning green = the short-term direction may have flipped.
• Common use: add up the bar area of two same-direction moves and compare. If the later area is clearly smaller, call it divergence.

**How this app does it**

• **MACD bar area is how trend divergence is judged**: if the c leg (leaving the pivot) has a smaller area than the b leg (between the two pivots), that is divergence and the basis of a type-1 buy / sell.
• On the detail page, the MACD panel shades the b leg and the c leg in pink so you can compare the bar areas of the two legs; the area ratio is also labeled on the main chart.

title: The Three Buy/Sell Points
summary: 1st buy catches the bottom, 2nd confirms it, 3rd follows strength — later is more certain, but pricier
body:
**The diagram**

First a downtrend: two pivots stepping lower. After leaving the second pivot, price makes a new low but falls less than the previous leg (bottom divergence). That's the **1st buy**. After the bounce, the first pullback holds above the 1st-buy low: the **2nd buy**. Later price leaves a new pivot upward, and the first pullback doesn't return into it: the **3rd buy**. Sell points are the mirror image.

**Textbook definition**

• **1st buy**: the low of a bottom divergence after a downtrend (at least two pivots stepping lower without overlap). Divergence inside a range doesn't count.
• **2nd buy**: the **first** pullback after the 1st buy that stays above the 1st-buy low.
• **3rd buy**: the **first** pullback after price leaves a pivot upward, staying above the pivot top without returning into it.
• The 1st buy is cheapest but fails most often; the 3rd is most certain but furthest from the bottom.

**How this app does it**

The analysis page, the radar and lower-level confirmation use the same rules, following the textbook definitions above:

• **1st buy**: the low of a trend divergence (at least two pivots stepping lower without overlap before it). Under the Strict rule, divergence inside a range doesn't count; the default Balanced rule also counts it as a 1st buy (Relaxed counts more). Switch under Me → Preferences → Signal rules. Divergence is measured by MACD bar area, comparing the leg that leaves the last pivot with the leg between the two pivots.
• **2nd buy**: the first pullback after the 1st buy that doesn't break the 1st-buy low.
• **3rd buy**: the first pullback after price leaves a pivot upward whose low stays above the pivot top, without returning into it.
• If one stroke end qualifies as both a 2nd and a 3rd point, only the 3rd is kept. Sell points are the mirror image.
• Under the Strict and Balanced rules, buy/sell points only sit on **finished strokes** (the Relaxed rule also shows signals on the last stroke early; a ✓ on the bubble means the stroke is finished). While the last stroke is still unfolding its end may extend or even fall back into the pivot, so what appears there is a gray dashed badge with a "pending" mark (e.g. "Pending 3rd sell"). It is not yet a buy/sell point and isn't counted in the buy/sell totals. Red and green are reserved for established points.

**Dates, invalidation and strength**

• On the chart a signal sits at the end of its stroke (the extreme candle); the date in the list and on the radar is the day the signal was **established** — the day the next stroke from that end first takes shape — which can be several candles, even weeks, after the chart marker. The dashed line with a small circle and the "Formed" label marks that day.
• If that stroke later extends (price keeps making new lows or highs), the signal becomes invalid and disappears.
• A type-1 divergence either holds or it doesn't, with no strength tiers; types 2 and 3 are judged by how solid the previous finished pivot is and how far the pullback stays from its edge.
• These are structural readings, not investment advice.

title: Levels and Lower-Level Confirmation
summary: The higher level sets direction, the lower level finds entries; level comes from nested pivots, and timeframes are only an approximation
body:
**The diagram**

The thick orange line is one up-stroke on the higher level. Zoom in and it's made of many small blue strokes, with its own pivot and a 3rd buy. The lower-level 3rd buy points the same way as the higher level, which is an "aligned" signal.

**Textbook definition**

• Level is defined by pivots nested inside each other: lower-level moves form pivots, and those build the next level up.
• Using timeframes (30-minute, daily, weekly) as levels is a practical approximation, not the strict definition.
• **Nested intervals**: once the higher level shows a direction, go one level down to find a more precise entry. Signals are most reliable when both levels agree.
• Match the signal to your holding period: using a 30-minute buy for a months-long position is the wrong tool for the job.

**How this app does it**

• The analysis page switches between daily and weekly. For the bigger picture, switch to weekly.
• Lower-level confirmation goes one step down, never skipping: **daily with 30-minute** (last 2 trading days) and **weekly with daily** (last two weeks).
• The higher-level direction comes from the detail page's pattern conclusion. Bullish + a lower-level buy = **aligned buy**; bearish + a sell = **aligned sell**; opposite directions = **counter-trend**, usually just a lower-level bounce or pullback; no lower-level signal or no clear direction = **waiting**.
• So the structure doesn't shift with your chosen start date, daily analysis always uses the latest two years (plus one more year loaded as warm-up), and your start date only decides which part is shown; weekly loads about 540 extra days and 30-minute 20 extra days, computed on the full history and then trimmed.
